Article.ArticleTitle: Semaglutide modulates explore/exploit decision-making in major depressive disorder: A randomized clinical trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Explore/exploit decision-making is a crucial component of motivated behavior. Explore/exploit behaviors are related to disparate cognitive and reward-related functions and have been implicated in multiple neuropsychiatric conditions, including major depressive disorder (MDD). Several mediators of explore/exploit decision-making have been proposed; metabolic mechanisms have been theorized to potentially affect its underlying processes. Here, we examined the effects of a GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA), semaglutide, on explore/exploit behavior in patients with MDD, using a four-armed restless bandit task.

In this secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial, 72 participants with MDD were randomized either to oral semaglutide (n = 35) or placebo (n = 37), and completed the bandit task at baseline and following 16 weeks of treatment. Explore/exploit decision-making was assessed using computational modeling of choice behavior, with a trial-by-trial reinforcement-learning model.

Treatment with semaglutide resulted in increased exploitation (i.e. choosing the option with the highest expected reward) (Average Treatment Effect [ATE] = 0.0242, p < 0.001), directed exploration (i.e. exploring a choice with higher uncertainty) (ATE = 0.0619, p = 0.013), and perseveration (i.e. the value-independent tendency to repeat the previous action) (ATE = 0.3017, p = 0.013). These effects were moderated by, but ultimately independent of, baseline characteristics and weight loss during the trial.

Treatment with semaglutide modulated explore/exploit behaviors in patients with MDD. These results highlight the role of metabolic mechanisms in decision-making processes in MDD and expand knowledge of the potential neuropsychiatric effects of GLP-1RAs.

Journal.Title: Journal of diabetes and its complications

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of semaglutide and empagliflozin on markers of endothelial function in persons with type 2 diabetes: A post hoc analysis of a randomized clinical trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: The endothelium maintains vascular health by regulating blood flow and protecting against inflammatory damage. In type 2 diabetes (T2DM), however, hyperglycemia, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia place a significant burden on the endothelium, potentially leading to atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease (CVD). While semaglutide and empagliflozin have been shown to reduce CVD risk in T2DM, it remains unclear whether these benefits are mediated by improved endothelial function. This post-hoc analysis explores the effects of these agents on markers of endothelial function, i.e. the reactive hyperaemic index (RHI) and the endothelial-derived cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) E-Selectin, ICAM-1, P-Selectin, and VCAM-1.

This was a post-hoc analysis of a 32-week randomized trial evaluating the separate and combined effects of semaglutide and empagliflozin on cardio-renal organ damage. One hundred and twenty participants with type 2 diabetes, age ≥ 50 were randomized to four groups (semaglutide, empagliflozin, the combination or placebo). An increase in RHI and/or a decrease in CAMs were considered beneficial.

RHI increased compared to baseline (0.11, 95%CI [0.008;0.21], p = 0.03) but not compared to placebo in the semaglutide group (0.11, 95%CI [-0.04;0.24], p = 0.16). There was no effect on RHI in the empagliflozin group. Compared to placebo, E-Selectin decreased significantly in the semaglutide and combination groups (-9, 95%CI [-14.1;-5.1] p < 0.01 and - 9, 95%CI [-14.3; -5.2] p < 0.01, respectively). VCAM-1 increased in the same groups, compared to placebo (12.3, 95%CI[2.8;20.8] p = 0.01 and 16.2, 95%CI [7.2;24.3], p < 0.01, respectively).P-Selectin and ICAM-1 was not significantly affected in any of the groups, compared to placebo (p ≥ 0.11 and p ≥ 0.09, respectively).

Semaglutide improved endothelial function compared to baseline, but not significantly versus placebo, which likely is due to limited power. CAM responses were heterogeneous, suggesting distinct roles in endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis. ClinicalTrialsRegister.eu: EudraCT 2019-000781-38.
